stem: A metal finishing shop generates a rinse water with a pH of 1.4. It contains no listed chemicals. Is it hazardous waste?

choices.text: No — it isn't on any EPA list
Yes — it exhibits the corrosivity characteristic
No — pH is not a regulated property
Yes — but only if it also fails the TCLP test

feedback: A waste is hazardous if it's listed or if it exhibits any characteristic. A pH of 1.4 falls below the corrosivity threshold of 2.0, so the rinse water is a characteristic hazardous waste on its own. It doesn't need to appear on a list, and it doesn't need to fail any additional test. Re-study block 4 (S-04, corrosivity).

stem: A waste liquid has a flash point of 118°F. Under RCRA it is:

choices.text: Non-hazardous, because the threshold is 100°F
Hazardous — it exhibits the ignitability characteristic
Hazardous only if it also appears on the F-list
Regulated under Subtitle D as municipal solid waste

feedback: The ignitability threshold for liquids is a flash point below 140°F (60°C). At 118°F the waste falls under that limit and is a characteristic hazardous waste. Listing is a separate, independent route to the same result — a waste needs only one.

stem: What does the Toxicity Characteristic Leaching Procedure simulate?

choices.text: Combustion of waste in an incinerator
Absorption of waste through human skin
Conditions inside a landfill, where water percolates through buried waste
Long-term atmospheric weathering of exposed waste

feedback: The TCLP recreates the acidic, wet conditions of a landfill to determine whether regulated contaminants would leach out of the waste and reach groundwater. This is why a waste can be stable, non-flammable, and pH-neutral, yet still be hazardous by the toxicity characteristic.

stem: Why can't a generator dilute a listed waste to escape regulation?

choices.text: Dilution always raises the pH above 12.5
A listed waste remains hazardous regardless of concentration
Dilution is only prohibited for large quantity generators
Diluted wastes automatically become P-listed

feedback: The two doors into Subtitle C work differently. Characteristic wastes are defined by how the waste behaves, so treatment can in principle change that. Listed wastes are hazardous by identity, and remain so through dilution — which is precisely why the listing system exists alongside the characteristics.

stem: Under RCRA, what makes a waste legally hazardous?

choices.text: A chemist's professional judgment that it is dangerous
It exhibits one of four characteristics, or it appears on one of four lists
Only its appearance, by name, on an EPA list
Being generated by any industrial process

feedback: The definition is legal, not scientific: a waste is hazardous if it meets the definition in 40 CFR Part 261, and there are exactly two doors in — exhibiting a characteristic, or appearing on a list. Either one alone is enough. Re-study block 1 (S-01).

stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the four hazardous waste characteristics?

choices.text: Ignitability
Radioactivity
Reactivity
Toxicity

feedback: The four characteristics are ignitability, corrosivity, reactivity, and toxicity, carrying waste codes D001 through D043. Radioactivity is regulated under other statutes, not 40 CFR Part 261. Re-study block 2 (S-02).

stem: Why is the reactivity characteristic (D003) harder to apply than the other three?

choices.text: Its criteria are narrative — there is no single laboratory test
It applies only to wastes that are also listed
It requires running the TCLP twice
Its flash point threshold changes with altitude

feedback: Reactivity's criteria are narrative — normally unstable, water-reactive, explosive, or cyanide/sulfide bearing — so there is no sample you can send out for a yes-or-no answer. That is why generator knowledge matters most here: somebody has to know what is in the drum. Re-study block 5 (S-05).

stem: A discarded, unused commercial chemical is acutely hazardous. Which list carries it, and with what quantity threshold?

choices.text: The P list, with a one-kilogram monthly threshold
The U list, with the same threshold as any other waste
The F list, because the source is non-specific
The K list, if the generator's industry is named

feedback: Discarded unused commercial chemicals go on the P list when acutely hazardous and the U list when merely toxic, and the P list carries the far lower one-kilogram threshold. The F and K lists cover process wastes, not discarded products. Re-study block 7 (S-07).
